title: The Lease in Kitengela and the Urinals Penda Health Had Removed
dek: At the end of 2011 three co-founders put in more of their own money, sold $100 loans to friends and readied a cheap clinic beside Kenya's largest industrial zone.

story.founder: Stephanie Koczela, Nick Sowden, Beatrice Ngoche
story.event: Funding and opening the first low-cost women's health clinic in Kitengela
story.summary: In late 2011 Penda Health's co-founders Stephanie Koczela, Nick Sowden and Beatrice Ngoche chose not to wait for impact investors: they put in more of their own money and sold 150 'Social Shares', $100 unsecured loans to the first clinic, and signed a lease in Kitengela, next to Kenya's largest industrial zone. The clinic opened in February 2012 with fees planned well below those of other private clinics; by July it had seen more than 1,300 patients, and in August six investors put in $100,000.
paragraphs: On 29 December 2011, Penda Health signed the lease on its first clinic, in Kitengela town centre, about half an hour from Nairobi and next to Kenya's largest industrial zone. The co-founders, Stephanie Koczela, Nick Sowden and Beatrice Ngoche, had met that June, drawn together by the demand for family planning in Kenya. Ngoche started researching that week and, Sowden wrote, met more than 1,000 women. The plan was a chain of clinics offering women comprehensive care at very low cost, with a focus on sexual and reproductive health.

The money had looked short. Impact investors were interested but slow, and raising on an idea, before any clinic existed, would mean a poor valuation. "Over a hard few days in New York City, we measured our confidence in the business and decided to double down," Sowden wrote. Having already spent about $8,000 of their own money working unpaid, each founder put in more. When a Facebook post brought 29 offers of $100 in a day, Koczela proposed "Social Shares": unsecured loans to the first clinic alone, repayable from its profits with interest after two years. In three weeks they sold 150, more than the roughly $13,000 they had projected the clinic needed.

Then came the room. Koczela listed what it needed: more sockets, better lighting, working toilets and plumbing, paint, tiles, and the removal of urinals fixed in the open in the shared bathroom, which the landlords agreed to take out. The plan was three examination rooms, a small pharmacy, a small laboratory and a large reception. A survey of 16 private, mission and charity clinics had found an average consultation fee of 540 shillings; Penda pencilled in 200.

The clinic opened in February 2012. By May it had seen more than 400 patients, Koczela said; by July, managers put the figure above 1,300, with a quarter of visitors returning. Ngoche explained the pull simply: "At government hospitals, nurses are rude, queues are long. That should not happen to patients." In August six investors, including the Eleos Foundation, put in $100,000.

quote.text: However faded the tea-room and the tea-equipage may seem, everything is absolutely clean. Not a particle of dust will be found in the darkest corner, for if any exists the host is not a tea-master.
quote.source_title: The Book of Tea, Project Gutenberg eBook #769
quote.connection: Okakura's tea-room is plain and faded on purpose, yet nothing in it may be dirty. Penda's founders set fees far below other clinics but would not open until the light, the plumbing and the bathroom were fit for the women they hoped would walk in.

reflection: The urinals had stood in that bathroom long enough for nobody to notice them. It took someone picturing a particular patient, a woman coming off a factory shift, walking through the door, to see that the room as it was would tell her she was not expected.

Most of us have a space like that: a desk, a reception corner, a kitchen at home, a form people fill in. Low cost and modesty are not the problem. The problem is the one awkward thing everyone has stopped seeing, which a newcomer sees in the first minute.
invitation: Walk through one space you look after today as if you were arriving for the first time. Note the single thing a stranger would find awkward, and fix it or ask whose job it is.

cross_checks.claim: Penda Health's co-founders were Stephanie Koczela, Nick (Nicholas) Sowden and Beatrice Ngoche.
The first clinic was in Kitengela and opened in February 2012.
The first clinic was financed partly by 'Social Shares', $100 loans from individual supporters repaid from the clinic's profits with interest after two years.
The clinic had seen more than 400 patients by May 2012 and more than 1,300 by July 2012.

research_notes: Founders: the slate named 'Stephanie Weber and co-founders'. No source found names a Stephanie Weber. Penda's own 2011-2012 blog (posts signed by Stephanie Koczela and Nick Sowden, and Sowden's 'All 3 cofounders'), VC4A (May 2012) and NextBillion (July 2012) name the co-founders as Stephanie Koczela, Nicholas (Nick) Sowden and Beatrice Ngoche; VC4A's May article spells the surname 'Kozcela' and its February article 'Koczela', as does her own blog byline, so 'Koczela' is used. VC4A (February 2012) also lists Dr Job Makoyo as a team member, not a co-founder. A Kenya Times profile naming a 'Jonathan Petrides' as co-founder is unsupported elsewhere and not used. Opening date: the founders' 30 December 2011 post planned a 30 January opening; NextBillion says the clinic opened in January; Koczela told VC4A in May 2012 that it opened in February, and VC4A's February 2012 article says she opened it that week (placing it loosely 'in Nairobi'); the story uses February 2012, the founder's own later statement. Social Shares terms: Sowden's blog gives 10% annual interest; NextBillion reports 5% over two years; the story says only 'with interest'. Amount: Sowden says 150 shares sold, more than the roughly $13,000 projected for the first clinic; NextBillion says $20,000 was needed per clinic; the story uses the founder's figure and attributes it as a projection. Patients: VC4A (May) over 400, NextBillion (July) over 1,300; these are different dates, not a conflict. Prices: the January 2012 blog survey gives an average consultation of 540 shillings and a potential Penda price of 200; Business Daily reported Sh150 by December 2012; the story gives the planned 200 only. Distance from Nairobi: VC4A says half an hour, NextBillion an hour; the story uses VC4A. Founders' own-money total (about $8,000) adds Sowden's '3k or less' and '5k or so'. Penda's individual 2011-2012 blog posts are not archived separately; the 11 February 2012 Internet Archive snapshot of the blog homepage contains all four posts cited. Funding is set to 'mixed' (founders' own money, friends' loans, then impact investors) rather than the slate's 'venture'. The Book of Tea passage describes the tea-room's cleanliness; it is applied by analogy.
